text: A healthcare provider will send patient transcripts containing PHI to Claude. The provider has signed a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). What must the architect still do before building?
options: Confirm each feature and model in the design is covered by the BAA and ZDR terms
Nothing more, because a signed BAA covers every API feature and every model
Add a system prompt telling Claude not to repeat patient identifiers in outputs
Rely on prompt cache expiry to delete PHI, so no further retention design is needed
correct_answer: Confirm each feature and model in the design is covered by the BAA and ZDR terms
explanation: A BAA does not cover everything: eligibility for HIPAA and Zero Data Retention varies by feature and model, and features that keep state on the provider's side are the usual exceptions. The architect checks each feature and model against current eligibility (A). Assuming full coverage (B) is the classic trap. A prompt instruction (C) is not a compliance control. Cache expiry (D) is irrelevant; the retention risk lives in your own logs, datasets, and indexes.

text: A knowledge assistant must never show HR salary documents to employees outside HR. Which control is preventive?
options: An audit log of every document the assistant retrieves, reviewed weekly by security
A confirmation prompt that asks the user to confirm they are allowed to see HR files
An access-control filter at retrieval time, so salary documents never reach the model
A system prompt instruction telling Claude to keep salary information confidential
correct_answer: An access-control filter at retrieval time, so salary documents never reach the model
explanation: A preventive control makes the bad outcome impossible: filtering retrieval by the user's access rights (C) means salary chunks never enter the context. An audit log (A) is detective and only finds the leak afterward. A confirmation prompt (B) is compensating and leaves the documents reachable. A prompt instruction (D) is not a control at all, because the documents are already in the model's context.

text: A research agent browses public web pages, can query the internal customer database, and can post results to any webhook URL. Which change best removes the data-exfiltration risk?
options: Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to ignore instructions found on web pages
Restrict outbound posting to an approved list of internal webhook destinations
Log every webhook call and alert security when an unknown URL is used
Switch to a more capable model that is better at spotting manipulation
correct_answer: Restrict outbound posting to an approved list of internal webhook destinations
explanation: Private data, untrusted content, and a way to send data out form the lethal trifecta; the defense is to break one leg structurally. Restricting outbound posting to approved destinations (B) removes the exfiltration path. A prompt rule (A) is not a leg-breaker. Logging (C) is detective and only shows the leak afterward. A larger model (D) can still be manipulated.

text: An agent can perform the four actions below. Using risk and reversibility, which one needs a human to approve it before it runs?
options: Adding draft topic tags to internal support tickets
Writing claim summaries that an adjuster finalizes later
Bulk-updating CRM fields, with a snapshot taken first for rollback
Permanently deleting a customer's account and its data
correct_answer: Permanently deleting a customer's account and its data
explanation: Human-in-the-loop approval belongs on actions that are both high impact and hard or impossible to reverse, such as permanent account deletion (D). Draft tags (A) are low impact and easy to reverse, so they can be automated with sampling. Claim summaries (B) already get human review afterward. Bulk updates with a snapshot (C) are reversible, so automation with alerts and fast rollback fits.

text: A support agent sometimes cites policy clauses that do not exist in the knowledge base. Legal wants this stopped before answers reach customers. Which guardrail targets the failure most directly?
options: Check each citation against the retrieved sources before the answer is sent
Move to a larger model tier, which is less likely to invent policy citations
Add a disclaimer to every answer saying that policies may have changed
Sample 5% of answers each week for review by the legal team
correct_answer: Check each citation against the retrieved sources before the answer is sent
explanation: A grounding check that verifies each citation against the retrieved sources before the response is returned (A), with a fallback such as "I could not confirm this", stops invented citations from reaching customers. A larger model (B) reduces but does not eliminate hallucination. A disclaimer (C) does not prevent the wrong answer. Weekly sampling (D) is detective and finds problems only after customers have seen them.
